title: Brain Training Works. Just Not the Way You Hoped.
author: Child Development Matters
summary: This short essay from Child Development Matters examines the claim that brief daily brain-training games sharpen memory and attention. It argues that the games do work, but only on the specific task practised, because practice changes narrow networks in the brain rather than the brain as a whole. The author cites the largest online training test, with more than eleven thousand people, in which participants improved on trained tasks and not at all on untrained ones, and a pooled look at nearly ninety working-memory studies that found no far transfer to reasoning or schoolwork. Examples from musicians, number-span practice and chess masters show how skill stays welded to what was practised. A review of the evidence cited by training companies found strong support only for the trained task. The essay concludes that the best broad lift to the mind is ordinary schooling, meaning effortful learning that is always a little too hard.
points: Brain-training games improve performance on the trained task but do not transfer to distant tasks, reasoning or everyday memory.
Practice is local rather than general, so the brain behaves less like one muscle and more like many separate skills.
A chess master recalls real positions almost perfectly but is barely better than a novice on random piece placements, which shows how skill is tied to what was practised.
A large review of the companies' own best evidence found strong support for the trained task, thinner support for related tasks and almost none for everyday life.
Broad, effortful schooling that is slightly too hard is the best-supported route to a generally sharper mind, so parents can skip the apps.
quotes: Here is the part the advert leaves out. The games work. That was never the problem. The problem is what they work on.
By the end, people had gotten better at every task they practised. On the tasks they had not practised, even ones that looked like close cousins of the trained games, nothing had moved at all.

When you drill a task, the brain genuinely changes, but it changes in a stubbornly specific place. The networks that particular task leans on get more efficient, and the gain stays bolted to them, doing that one job.

Show a chess master a real game position for a few seconds, and they will rebuild it from memory almost perfectly. Scatter the same pieces at random, and they are barely better than someone who learned the moves last week.

Gather up nearly ninety of those studies and the picture holds still. Train, and your scores on the working-memory tasks go up, at least for a while. But the jump everyone is actually paying for, into sharper reasoning and better schoolwork, never arrives.
Getting fast and accurate at chopping an onion makes you good at chopping onions. It does not travel across to your handwriting, even though both are just your hand.
Year after year of broad, effortful learning that is always a little too hard, the kind that makes a child think in ways they would never have picked for themselves. No game has come close.
